title: Serving without burning out
hook: the acrobat's balance: care for yourself too (SN 47.19)
tomorrow: Mai's been asked to teach little kids. what can a walk teach first?

segments.voice: Yesterday, serving in hard places: the Buddha walked toward Angulimala, and the man everyone fled could stop. Today the week comes back, with a question about how long anyone can keep giving.
screen: `HARD PLACES.` → `HOW LONG CAN ANYONE KEEP GIVING?`

segments.voice: Running on empty can start to feel like proof you care: the late night, the yes to every ask, the quick "i'm fine" text. Mai has had that week. The mural on art day. Water and company for Jess through the fever. Ten minutes at the creek that turned into an afternoon. And last night, art cards for the county jail until almost two. This morning she fell asleep in studio with a brush in her hand, and she hasn't sat on her own once all week. The suttas answer her with a balancing act: two acrobats, one bamboo pole, and an argument about who keeps whom from falling.
screen: `RUNNING ON EMPTY.` → `A WEEK OF YES.` → `TWO ACROBATS, ONE POLE.`

segments.voice: The Buddha tells it near a town called Sedaka. An acrobat sets up his bamboo pole and calls his apprentice to climb up and stand on his shoulders. Then he lays out the plan. You look after me, and I'll look after you. Guarded by each other, we'll show our skill, earn our fee, and come down safe. The apprentice says no. Teacher, you look after yourself, and I'll look after myself. Each of us guarded by our own care, we'll show our skill and come down safe. And the Buddha says the apprentice has it right. Guarding yourself, you guard others. Guarding others, you guard yourself. Then he names both halves. You guard yourself by sati, mindfulness, practiced, developed and made much of. You guard others by patience, by not harming, by loving-kindness, metta, and by sympathy. That's the teaching, and the story is kept among the Buddha's sayings on mindfulness. In this sutta, keeping your own practice isn't time taken away from caring. It's the footing the care stands on. A teacher who loses his balance drops the one on his shoulders. Run the week back through that. A question asked on a street. A lamp of your own. A path turned outward. A sick monk washed. A tree left standing. A road toward the man everyone fled. Every one of those needed someone standing steady. For Mai, the jail cards are real care. So is the sit she skipped.
screen: `"YOU WATCH ME, I'LL WATCH YOU."` · `"EACH OF US WATCHES OUR OWN."` · `MINDFULNESS GUARDS; KINDNESS GUARDS.` · `A WEEK OF SERVING.` · then, large: `BALANCE.`

segments.voice: Set down whatever you're holding: the phone, the pen, the brush. Choose one sound near you, a fan, traffic, your own breath, and let your attention rest on it, the way an acrobat's weight settles on one steady foot. When the mind runs to the list of what's still owed, come back to the sound.
Serving without burning out: keeping your own footing so the care can go on. The acrobat's apprentice minded their own footing, and so kept both of them up.
Carry this: balance. Keep your own footing, and the one on your shoulders stays up. A week of serving, done.

howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers who train chaplains and volunteers ask them to keep a daily sit alongside their service, and the acrobat story from the Samyutta Nikaya is one they tell.

fork.setup: at art day, a kid paints right over the corner you spent an hour on, and your jaw tightens. by the acrobat sutta, what guards you here?

fork.reveal: the Buddha says guarding others, by patience, harmlessness, kindness and sympathy, is also how you guard yourself. the patient answer keeps your own mind steady.

original.note: Pali: mindfulness; in the acrobat sutta, the way you guard yourself.

trapdoor: what you thought: looking after yourself is a break from serving others.

what a scholar hears: SN 47.19 sits in the Satipatthana Samyutta, the connected sayings on mindfulness; the self-guard is mindfulness developed, the other-guard is patience, harmlessness, loving-kindness and sympathy.
guess: keeping your own footing so you can keep helping
putting others first until there's nothing left
stepping back from helping until you feel ready

chat.meaning: In SN 47.19 the Buddha sides with the apprentice: guarding yourself by mindfulness is how you guard others, so Mai's sit holds up her service.

tie.story: The acrobat's apprentice said each should guard their own footing, and the Buddha agreed: guarding yourself, you guard others.
tie.friend: Mai can come back to her sit this week; it's what keeps her steady enough to keep making the cards.
tie.you: what keeps your footing steady when you're giving a lot?

notes: SN 47.19 paraphrased: among the Sumbhas at Sedaka, the Buddha tells of an acrobat who sets up his bamboo pole and has his apprentice climb up and stand on his shoulders; the teacher proposes 'you protect me and I'll protect you'; the apprentice answers that each should protect himself, and so they will show their skill, get their fee and come down safely; the Buddha says that is the method: protecting oneself one protects others (by pursuing, developing and cultivating mindfulness), protecting others one protects oneself (by patience, harmlessness, loving-kindness and sympathy). Confirm the compression; the apprentice's name (Medakathalika) is left out because translators differ on its form and gender.
'this story sits in the suttas' chapter on mindfulness': SN 47 is the Satipatthana Samyutta; confirm the wording.
howItsDone is a general description (teachers of Buddhist volunteers and chaplains encouraging their own practice; the story told in that setting), not from the cited text; confirm or soften.
